title: 529 Plan Real Estate Strategies to Help Fund College Costs
summary: Learn how a 529 plan works, its tax advantages, and how real estate may complement a 529 college savings plan to help fund college costs.
body_markdown:
Rising college costs are challenging parents, property owners, and[real estate investors](https://www.cbiz.com/industries/real-estate) to think beyond traditional savings accounts. For those who already own or are considering investment property, real estate can complement a 529 plan and create added flexibility when education funding is part of a broader tax and[financial strategy](https://www.cbiz.com/insights/article/finding-a-wealth-advisor-who-aligns-with-your-goals) . Learn how 529 plans work, where real estate fits into college savings planning, and what investors should consider before using property as part of an education funding strategy.


## What Is a 529 Plan?


529 plans are education savings plans designed to help pay for a beneficiary’s qualified education expenses. These expenses can include tuition, fees, books, supplies, equipment, and, for students enrolled at least half-time, room and board. While commonly used for college, 529 plans can also apply to K-12 tuition (up to $20,000 per year), certain related expenses, apprenticeship programs, qualified student loan repayments (up to $10,000), and certain postsecondary credentialing expenses.


Contributions aren’t federally tax-deductible, but earnings grow tax-free, and withdrawals are generally tax-free when used for qualified expenses. Many states also offer tax deductions or credits for contributions.


## How Real Estate Can Support College Savings


Real estate can be an effective long-term strategy to diversify a household’s portfolio. For college savings, one approach is to purchase rental property when a child is young, allow it to appreciate over time, and later sell it to fund education expenses.


During the holding period, the owner may benefit from rental income, depreciation, deductible expenses, and potential capital gains treatment when the property is sold. If the child ultimately doesn’t attend college, the property owner can still retain the tax and investment benefits tied to the real estate asset.


However, real estate works differently from a 529 plan. Properties don’t receive the same tax-free growth and withdrawal treatment as a 529 account.


Real estate also comes with market risk, maintenance costs, financing considerations, insurance, property taxes, and tenant-management responsibilities. Investors should evaluate whether the anticipated appreciation, rental income, and tax benefits align with their timeline, liquidity needs, and broader financial plan.


## Using a 529 Plan for Room and Board With Real Estate Planning


Property owners should also consider how the room-and-board portion of qualified higher education expenses fits into their planning. Room and board can include on-campus and off-campus housing for students enrolled at least half-time. A 529 plan can’t be used to purchase real estate without triggering federal income taxes and a 10% penalty on the earnings portion of the withdrawal.


However, property owners can purchase property near campus using other funds and have the student pay fair market rent. Those rent payments can then help cover the mortgage.


For off-campus housing, tax-free 529 withdrawals are generally limited to the room-and-board allowance in the school’s published cost of attendance. This ensures qualified expenses match what the school determines is reasonable for housing and meals. If actual off-campus costs exceed the school’s allowance, account owners should plan carefully before using 529 funds for the excess amount.


## Planning Considerations for Real Estate Investors


Before pairing a real estate strategy with education savings, investors should consider cash flow, financing, holding period, rental demand, and timing of a sale. Properties near college campuses can attract rental demand, but often require more active management and careful documentation if occupied by family members. Investors should also consider how a sale could affect their tax position in the year education expenses are due.


Recordkeeping is especially important. Account owners should document fair market rent, lease terms, mortgage payments, eligible 529 withdrawals, and the school’s published cost of attendance. These records can help substantiate qualified expenses and support tax reporting if questions arise later.


## Why Coordination Matters


Real estate and 529 plans can both support education funding, but they work best when coordinated within a broader tax and financial strategy. Investors should understand how each option affects liquidity, tax exposure, timing, and long-term goals before using real estate as part of a college savings plan.


Those who own or are considering investment property should consult tax and financial advisors before making withdrawals, purchasing property, or transferring funds. To learn how these strategies may fit into your financial plan, connect with amember of our real estate team .
